processing: Orthodox black tea, sold as Orange Pekoe and long-leaf FOP grades; the estate also makes orthodox green and oolong.
harvest_season: Picking dates for this estate are not well documented; Nilgiri gardens crop across much of the year, with a peak after the spring rains.
appearance_liquor: Clear bright amber to reddish-gold, as is typical of Nilgiri black tea.
taste_profile: As with other high Nilgiri teas, expect a clean, fragrant and brisk cup, lighter than Assam; detailed notes on this estate are sparse.

brewing.notes: Western-style, with water slightly below the boil to keep the fragrance. Taste before adding milk or sugar.

vintage_note: Sold mainly by grade under the estate name, more often than by dated flush. Nilgiri black tea is usually bought as recent stock and drunk within a year or two; it is not an ageing tea.
description:
Chamraj is a high-altitude Nilgiri estate belonging to United Nilgiri Tea Estates, known as one of the region's quality-minded orthodox producers. It is described as among the highest and oldest gardens in the hills, though altitude figures differ from one account to another.

A Fairtrade case study notes the commercial choice to keep making distinctive orthodox black, green and oolong teas here. That matters because many South Indian growers moved to CTC in the late twentieth century.

Specific tasting notes for this estate are thin, so go by what is typical of high Nilgiri tea: fragrant, clean and brisk, without Assam's heavy malt. Keep the water a touch below boiling and the steep under three minutes.

When buying, the estate's Orange Pekoe and FOP grades are the place to start. The estate is also reported to hold organic and Fairtrade certification, so check the pack for the marks.
history:
United Nilgiri Tea Estates was incorporated in August 1922, with Robert Stanes credited as founder, and a company history says it bought Chamraj and Rockland, with a small factory, in 1923. Sellers often give 1922 as the estate's own date, but that is the company's date; planting on the land must be older, though how much older is not documented.

The group, today made up of four estates, is known for ethical certification. Chamraj has stayed orthodox through decades when much of the region moved to CTC.
